summary.title: How X Window Managers Work, And How To Write One (Part I)
summary.one_liner: You learn how X window managers fit into the X client-server model, how they intercept window requests via substructure redirection and reparenting, and how compositing window managers work.
takeaways: X does not mandate a window manager; a window manager is a normal X client that gets special privileges via the X server.
A window manager intercepts layout requests for top level windows through substructure redirection on the root window, which also acts as a lock so only one runs per screen.
Reparenting puts application windows inside WM-created frame windows so the WM can draw decorations; some WMs (e.g., xmonad, dwm) skip reparenting.
Compositing WMs use the X Composite extension to render windows off-screen and combine them into an overlay for effects like translucency and animations.
Part II of the series walks through a basic reparenting, non-compositing window manager implementation.
summary.summary: The article explains the role of an X window manager in a Linux/BSD desktop, drawing on the Xlib Programming Manual (quoted heavily, with a recommendation to read it). It covers the X server/client model, the window tree rooted at the root window, and how substructure redirection lets a WM intercept requests for top level windows. It then describes reparenting and frame windows, contrasts reparenting and non-reparenting WMs with examples, and explains compositing via the Composite extension. The post is the first of a series and ends by previewing a code walkthrough of a basic reparenting, non-compositing WM.
